c.v: Figure 37.3-2 shows the format of pulse code in RAM.
Each pulse code contains a
16-bit

entry with two fields: "level" and "period". "level" (0 or 1) indicates a low-/high-level value was received or is going to be sent, while "period" points out the number of clock cycles (see Figure 37.3-1 clk_div) that the level lasts for.

blocks.alt: Figure 37.3-2. Format of Pulse Code in RAM

c.v: The minimum value for the period is zero (0) and is interpreted as a transmission end-marker.
For a non-zero period (i.e., not an end-marker), its value is limited by APB clock and
RMT
clock according to the equation below:
5 × T_apb_clk + 6 × T_rmt_sclk < period × T_clk_div (37.1)
Note: RMT clock and APB clock must satisfy the following relation:
1.5 × T_apb_clk < 9 × T_rmt_sclk (37.2)
According to the equation above and the frequency of rmt_sclk, the pulse width (i.e.,
period
× T_clk_div) able to be captured by RMT is limited as follows:
the minimum value of pulse width should be larger than (5 × T_apb_clk + 6 × T_rmt_sclk).
the maximum value of pulse width should be smaller than or equal to (the maximum period × the maximum T_clk_div), i.e., ((2^15 - 1) × the maximum T_rmt_sclk × 256).
For more information about rmt_sclk frequency, or APB_CLK frequency, see
Section 37.3.3
, or
